Maya's heart did a somersault, but she made herself walk over. She pressed the button to stop it. Nothing happened. She unplugged it — actually unplugged it, the cord hanging loose and dead on the floor.

The machine kept washing.

That was when she noticed the sock.

It was lying on top of the drum, inside the little glass door, though the door had never been opened. It was small and white with faded red dinosaurs on it. A little kid's sock.

The machine's window fogged up, the way they do with hot water. And in the fog, something wrote. Slowly, in wobbly letters like a kid just learning cursive:

**MY TURN**

Maya's mouth went dry. "I — I wasn't using that machine," she whispered. "It's all yours."

The letters faded. New ones appeared.

**LOST IT HERE. 1989. MOM NEVER FOUND IT. SHE CRIED.**

Maya sat down on the cold linoleum, right there in front of the machine, because her legs had stopped working. "You've been waiting since 1989? For a sock?"

**WASHING TAKES FOREVER WHEN YOU'RE ALONE.**

Something about that made her chest ache instead of her skin crawl. Maya thought of her own lucky socks, the ones with the stars, and how upset she'd be if she lost one.

"It's almost done," she said, watching the drum slow. "Do you want me to stay?"

The window fogged one more time.

**THANK YOU.**

The machine clicked, beeped, and stopped. Maya opened the door, and the sock was warm — the only warm thing in the whole laundromat. She folded it carefully, the way her mom folded things, and set it on top of the spider plant.

When her mom came back, the sock was gone. But the spider plant, which had been brown and crispy for as long as anyone could remember, had one small green leaf unfurling in the fluorescent light.

Maya still does her laundry at the grandma machine. She always brings two quarters extra, just in case somebody else is waiting for their turn.

Automated warehouse robots often get stuck repeatedly trying the same failed grip on difficult items, which slows down package sorting. Researchers developed new strategies that allow these robots to "remember" past mistakes and adjust their approach instead of repeating the error. This improved method more than doubled the number of successful picks per hour in real-world tests compared to previous systems.

This paper addresses a problem in warehouse robots that pick items from bins: sometimes a robot fails to grab an object, but because nothing changes in the bin, it keeps trying the exact same failed move repeatedly, wasting time. The researchers identified certain objects that are especially prone to this “stuck in a loop” failure and created a classification system for them. They then developed smarter robot decision-making strategies that remember past failures and adjust future attempts, and testing showed these strategies dramatically improved picking speed—more than doubling it in real-world trials.

This paper describes a computer system that reads a passage of text and answers questions by pinpointing the exact stretch of words in that passage that contains the answer. The author's main innovation is having the system first predict where an answer starts, then use that prediction to help figure out where it ends — a linked approach that, along with a scoring method favoring short, confident answers, improved performance by about 15%. On a standard reading comprehension test, the system gave an exactly correct answer about 65% of the time, with an overall answer-quality score of roughly 74%.

Researchers created a new computer mapping tool to figure out exactly how much sunlight reaches roads and parking lots throughout the year, which helps determine where solar-powered cars can recharge. Existing tools struggled to account for shadows from buildings or how leafy trees block more sun in summer than in winter, so the team developed a better method that factors in these changing conditions. By testing their approach in a North Carolina city and sharing the code publicly, they created detailed sunlight maps that can help drivers find sunny spots to charge electric vehicles or shady places to park regular cars.

Researchers have developed a new method to accurately map how much sunlight reaches roads and parking lots throughout the year, specifically accounting for shadows cast by buildings and seasonal changes in tree foliage. This tool helps urban planners optimize locations for charging solar-powered vehicles while also identifying shaded areas that could improve comfort for conventional drivers. By providing easy-to-use code and clear examples, the study makes this detailed solar analysis accessible for cities looking to improve transportation infrastructure.

This paper presents a new method for calculating how much sunlight reaches roads and parking lots, which matters for both solar-powered cars and keeping regular cars cool. The researchers improved existing mapping tools to better account for shadows from trees, including the fact that leafy trees block more sun in summer than in winter. They tested their approach in a North Carolina city and shared their code so others can use it to plan better parking and driving routes based on sun and shade.

Robots that pick items out of bins in e-commerce warehouses sometimes get stuck in a loop: if a grab fails and the bin looks unchanged, the robot keeps trying the exact same grip over and over on certain troublesome objects. The researchers identified the types of objects most prone to these repeated failures and designed new strategies that let the robot remember its past mistakes and deliberately try something different next time. In real-world tests, this "learn from failure" approach roughly doubled the number of successful picks per hour compared to the standard method.

Most AI tools designed to find unusual things look for obvious outliers, but this research introduces a new method for spotting hidden oddities that are buried within normal-looking data. The researchers tested their approach on simulated particle collisions from the Large Hadron Collider, trying to find evidence of undiscovered particles. Their method worked so well that it successfully detected a rare new particle hidden in just 0.08% of a million collision events, earning top marks in an international physics competition.

Most anomaly detection tools look for rare events that stand out from the norm, but this new method finds hidden patterns within common data that are statistically normal yet physically unique. The researchers applied this technique to particle collision data from the Large Hadron Collider and successfully identified a new particle that appeared in less than 0.1% of all events. This approach achieved top-tier results in a major scientific challenge by uncovering subtle signals that traditional methods might miss.

This paper introduces a new way to spot unusual patterns that don’t look like outliers but instead hide within normal-looking data. The method was tested on simulated particle collision data from the Large Hadron Collider, where it successfully identified a rare new particle appearing in fewer than one out of every thousand events. This approach performed better than existing methods in a competitive scientific challenge.

Researchers have created a new mapping method for estimating how much sunlight reaches roads and parking lots throughout the year, which matters both for charging solar-powered vehicles and for finding shady spots that keep conventional cars cooler. Existing mapping tools struggled to account for shadows from trees—especially deciduous trees that lose their leaves in autumn and let more light through in winter—so the team developed a technique that adjusts for these seasonal changes. After testing their approach in a North Carolina city and sharing the code publicly, they produced maps that can help drivers of solar vehicles find sunny spots to park and recharge, while also helping everyday drivers locate shade.

When training artificial intelligence, researchers use a technique called "dropout" to prevent the system from memorizing its training data instead of actually learning. This paper introduces a new version called "Sparseout," which gives researchers a simple way to control how many parts of the AI's brain are active versus turned off at any given time. The researchers found that this control is useful because different tasks prefer different setups: language-based AI works better when more of its internal connections are turned off (sparse), while image recognition works better when more connections stay on (dense).

Researchers have developed a new technique called Sparseout, which improves upon the common "dropout" method by allowing them to precisely control how many parts of an AI model are active at once. This adjustment helps prevent the model from memorizing data too closely and reveals that different tasks benefit from different levels of activity, with language processing preferring sparse models while image recognition works better with denser ones. Essentially, this tool gives scientists a more flexible way to tune neural networks for better performance on specific types of problems.

This paper introduces a new technique called Sparseout that helps control how many brain-like connections in a neural network are active at once, which can prevent the network from overfitting. The authors show mathematically that Sparseout is a more general version of a popular existing method called Dropout, and that it’s cheap to use in practice. By testing on language and image tasks, they found that language models work better with fewer active connections, while image models prefer more active ones—and Sparseout lets researchers easily tune this balance.

Training computers to understand spoken words usually requires huge amounts of recorded human speech, which is hard to come by for less common languages. This research explores whether artificially generated, computer-made voices can be used as practice material to help these systems learn without needing as much real-world audio. The researchers tested three different methods for creating this fake speech and found promising results that could lead to better voice-recognition technology in the future.

Researchers are exploring how to use computer-generated speech as extra training data to improve voice recognition systems, especially for languages that have very little recorded audio available. They tested three different methods of creating this synthetic speech to see if it could effectively replace the need for large amounts of real human recordings. The study found promising results, suggesting that high-quality synthesized voices can help build better speech recognition tools with fewer resources.

This paper explores whether computer-generated speech can help train speech recognition systems when there isn’t much real recorded speech available. The authors tested three types of artificial speech generators to see if adding their output to training data improves recognition. Their results suggest this approach is promising and could open up new ways to build speech recognizers with fewer real-world recordings.

As self-driving cars get closer to hitting the roads, researchers wanted to figure out what makes people trust—or distrust—them. They surveyed over 1,100 people about their feelings, knowledge, and concerns regarding automated vehicles, then used that information to train a smart computer program to predict how much someone would trust the technology. Unlike older methods that act like mysterious "black boxes," this new approach not only made highly accurate predictions but also clearly explained *why* it thought a person would or wouldn't trust a self-driving car.

Researchers surveyed over 1,000 people to understand what drives trust in self-driving cars by analyzing their knowledge, feelings, and experiences. They used a specialized machine learning model that not only predicts these trust levels accurately but also explains exactly which factors influence the predictions. This approach helps bridge the gap between complex technology and public acceptance by making it clear why people feel safe or unsafe around automated vehicles.

When training artificial neural networks, researchers commonly use a technique called "dropout," which randomly switches off some artificial neurons during training so the network doesn't just memorize its examples. This paper introduces a simple twist on that idea, called Sparseout, which adds a dial that lets researchers control exactly how many neurons stay quiet versus active—and it does this at almost no extra computational cost. Interestingly, when the authors tested it, they found that networks with many silent neurons performed better at language tasks (like predicting the next word), while image recognition worked best when more neurons stayed active.

Most machine learning anomaly detection looks for obviously strange outliers, but this new method instead hunts for groups of events that individually look normal yet together form an unexpected pattern hidden within ordinary data. The researchers applied their approach to simulated particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider to search for evidence of undiscovered particles. In a blind challenge where they didn't know the true answer beforehand, the method successfully detected a new particle appearing in only about 800 out of a million collision events, outperforming all competing approaches.

This study looks at what makes people trust self-driving cars, using a survey of over a thousand participants to measure things like their knowledge, feelings, and past experiences with the technology. The researchers then used a machine learning model to predict each person’s level of trust based on those survey answers, and they also used a special tool to explain which factors mattered most in those predictions. They found that their approach was better than older methods at both accurately predicting trust and clearly explaining why people feel the way they do about automated vehicles.

Researchers developed a new AI method called RANDPOL that uses simpler, randomly generated networks instead of complex, heavily tuned deep learning models to make decisions in continuous environments. This approach is cheaper and faster to train while actually improving performance compared to traditional methods. The study also provides mathematical guarantees on how well the algorithm works and demonstrates its effectiveness through testing on difficult tasks.

AI systems that learn by trial and error—like those used to master video games or teach robots to walk—usually rely on complex neural networks that require a huge amount of careful tuning. This paper introduces a new method called RANDPOL that uses "randomized" networks instead, which are faster to set up, cheaper to run, and actually perform better than the traditional approach. The researchers proved mathematically that their method works reliably within a specific timeframe and showed through experiments that it can handle difficult tasks just as well as standard AI techniques.

This paper introduces a new method for teaching computers to make decisions in complex, continuous situations (like controlling a robot or playing a video game). Instead of using the usual deep neural networks, which require a lot of time and effort to tune, the authors use simpler "randomized" networks that are cheaper to set up and actually work better. They prove mathematically that their method is reliable and show through experiments that it performs well compared to existing deep learning approaches.

Computers that transcribe speech normally need huge amounts of real recorded audio to learn from, but that kind of data is scarce for many languages and situations. This paper explores a workaround: using text-to-speech technology to generate artificial voice recordings, which then serve as extra "practice material" for training the speech recognition system. After testing three different voice-generation approaches, the authors found encouraging results, suggesting that synthetic speech could make it possible to build reliable speech recognizers with far less real-world data.

Researchers developed a new tool that analyzes travel reviews to identify specific phrases indicating whether a destination is suitable or unsuitable for people with unique needs, such as disabilities or dietary restrictions. By accurately detecting these inclusion and exclusion signals from user feedback, the system helps travelers avoid places that might not work for their personal situations. This advancement aims to make automated travel planning services more personalized and effective for everyone.

Travel apps can help you plan trips, but they often miss important details about whether a destination actually works for your specific needs—like if it’s wheelchair-accessible, offers vegan food, or is toddler-friendly. This paper introduces a computer program that automatically reads thousands of online reviews to pull out helpful phrases about who will and won’t be able to comfortably enjoy a particular place. The researchers found their tool was highly accurate at spotting these clues, which could eventually make travel planning apps much better at suggesting spots that truly fit each traveler's unique situation.

This paper addresses the problem that travel recommendation systems often ignore the specific needs of different visitors, such as those with disabilities, dietary restrictions, or young children. The researchers developed a method to automatically identify phrases in online reviews that indicate whether a tourist spot is welcoming (inclusion) or unwelcoming (exclusion) for people with 11 different characteristics. Their approach was tested on 2,000 reviews of 1,000 attractions and showed high accuracy in detecting these phrases, which could help make automated trip planners more personalized and inclusive.

Imagine a robot exploring an unknown area that needs to build an accurate map while simultaneously figuring out exactly where it is—a tough balancing act when every move involves guesswork. Traditional planning methods struggle because they try to calculate too many future possibilities, which slows the robot down as the environment gets bigger. To solve this, researchers taught the robot using advanced AI and trial-and-error in simulated worlds, allowing it to instantly make smart decisions about where to look next so it can explore quickly and map accurately in real time.

This research presents a new method for robots to efficiently map unknown environments by using advanced AI techniques called graph neural networks and deep reinforcement learning. Unlike older methods that struggle with complex tasks, this approach allows the robot to make fast, real-time decisions on where to look next without needing human help or pre-programmed instructions. As a result, the robot can create accurate maps more quickly and effectively than traditional systems.

This paper is about teaching a robot to explore and map an unknown area on its own. The robot needs to balance two goals: figuring out where it is and learning about new places around it. Traditional methods for this are too slow and complicated to work in real time, so the researchers used a type of artificial intelligence that learns from experience, like training a dog with treats. Their approach lets the robot make quick, smart decisions about where to go next, and it was tested successfully in a variety of simulated environments.

Travelers have very different needs—some use wheelchairs, some need vegetarian food, some are bringing a toddler—but most trip-planning tools don't account for whether attractions can actually accommodate them. The researchers built a computer system that reads online reviews of tourist spots and automatically picks out phrases indicating whether a place welcomes or turns away people with 11 different kinds of needs, like disabilities or dietary restrictions. The system proved highly accurate, and the authors believe it could help automatic itinerary apps plan trips that truly work for everyone.

Because fake news spreads so easily online, these researchers built an automated tool to help tell real news stories from false ones. Their system checks articles using three existing tools: one that rewrites text in different words, a grammar checker, and a program that analyzes how words relate to each other. When tested on known collections of real and fake news, this combined approach proved highly accurate and worked better across different topics than previous methods.

As self-driving cars move closer to everyday road use, one of the biggest hurdles to their adoption is whether the public trusts them—so this study set out to predict how much individual people trust the technology. The researchers surveyed over 1,100 people about their knowledge, feelings, past experiences, and views of the risks and benefits of automated vehicles, then fed that information into a machine learning model that predicted each person's level of trust. Crucially, they paired the model with a technique that explains which factors drove each prediction, allowing them to forecast trust accurately while also revealing what actually shapes it—something traditional statistics and opaque "black box" AI can't achieve together.

Researchers developed a new tool to automatically spot fake news by analyzing how articles are written, specifically looking at paraphrasing, grammar errors, and word choices. This method combines three common digital tools to identify subtle patterns that reveal whether a story is true or false. Tests show this approach is highly accurate and more reliable across different types of news than previous detection systems.

This paper introduces a new method for automatically spotting fake news by using three common digital tools: one that rewrites text, one that checks grammar, and one that analyzes word meanings. By combining clues from these tools, the researchers were able to identify patterns that distinguish real news from false stories. Their approach performed as well as or better than existing methods in tests, and it proved more reliable when applied to different types of news sources.

Modern face recognition systems are very accurate, but researchers have discovered they can be tricked by specially altered images. This paper introduces a new method that uses AI to dramatically change a person's photo—like giving them a completely different appearance—to fool the system into misidentifying them. The researchers found this trick worked about 80 to 90 percent of the time, and the fake photos looked so realistic that even built-in security defenses couldn't spot the manipulation.

Deep reinforcement learning—teaching computers to make good decisions through trial and error—has powered impressive successes in video games and robot control, but it usually depends on large neural networks that require painstaking fine-tuning to work well. The authors introduce a method called RANDPOL that instead uses "randomized" networks, in which most of the network's internal settings are fixed by chance and only a small portion is actually trained, making the approach cheaper and often more numerically stable for problems where situations and actions vary smoothly (like a robot's continuous movements). They also prove mathematical guarantees on how quickly the method reaches good performance, and show it holds its own against deep neural network approaches on challenging benchmark tasks.

Researchers have discovered a new way to trick face recognition systems by using AI image translation tools to completely alter a person's facial appearance, rather than just adding subtle noise. These modified images look realistic and still clearly show the original person’s identity, yet they successfully fool security systems in up to 90% of cases. This finding highlights that current defenses may be vulnerable to large-scale changes, raising concerns about the reliability of automated facial identification.

Face recognition systems powered by artificial intelligence are very accurate but can be tricked by specially altered images called adversarial examples. The authors developed a new way to create these deceptive images by using image translation, which lets them change a face to look like someone else while still appearing realistic. Their method successfully fooled face recognition systems about 90% of the time when they had full access to the system and 80% of the time when they didn’t, and the changes were large enough to defeat existing defenses.

This paper tackles how to get a mobile robot to explore and map an unfamiliar environment in real time, which requires it to choose where to point its sensors so that it both keeps track of where it is and learns as much as possible about its surroundings. Because traditional planning methods that simulate many possible future moves become far too slow as the problem grows larger, the authors instead trained an AI system—combining graph neural networks (which process information organized as networks of connected points) with reinforcement learning—to instantly recommend the robot's best next sensing action. This system trains itself automatically across many randomly generated environments with no human help, and the resulting decision-making is fast, scales well, and produces accurate maps while gathering information efficiently.

Researchers developed an automated system that uses a combination of different patient records to predict medical diagnosis codes, aiming to replace the slow and error-prone manual coding process. This new approach works better than previous methods by handling complex data more effectively and providing a confidence score for each prediction so users know how reliable it is. Tests on real hospital data showed the model can accurately predict primary diagnoses for both inpatients and outpatients, helping streamline billing and medical auditing.

When patients visit a hospital, their diagnoses must be translated into standardized medical codes for billing and record-keeping, but doing this manually is slow and difficult because clinical notes are often messy and there are thousands of possible codes. To solve this, researchers built an AI system that combines information from multiple parts of a patient's medical record to automatically predict the correct codes before the patient even leaves the hospital, while also indicating how confident the system is in its guesses. When tested on real patient data from a hospital in Thailand, the system successfully predicted the right diagnostic codes much of the time, showing promising potential to automate and speed up this important administrative task.

This paper describes a computer system that can automatically assign medical billing codes to patient records, a task normally done by hand. The researchers built a model that combines information from multiple parts of a patient’s file—not just the doctor’s discharge notes—to make more accurate predictions, and it also estimates how confident it is in each prediction. They tested the system on real hospital data from Thailand and found it performed reasonably well, especially for hospitalized patients, though there is still room for improvement.

This paper explores a security risk in advanced AI systems that learn by trial and error, showing that outsiders can secretly copy the AI’s decision-making process just by watching how it behaves. By repeatedly interacting with the AI and studying its responses, an attacker can build a working replica of it and potentially use that copy to manipulate or trick the original system. The researchers tested these attacks to prove they work and also discussed ideas for how developers might protect their AI from this kind of digital theft.

Face-recognition AI is now very accurate, but this research shows it can be fooled by realistic-looking fake images—not just the tiny, nearly invisible pixel changes that most security measures are built to detect. The researchers built a tool that transforms a photo of a face into a convincing new version of that face: the changes are big enough to slip past standard defenses, yet the image still looks like a real photo of the same person. In their tests, this trick fooled the face-recognition systems 80–90% of the time, revealing a serious weakness in how these systems are currently protected.

Researchers show that it is possible to secretly copy a smart AI agent’s decision-making rules by observing how it acts, much like learning a game strategy by watching an expert play. Once this copy is made, attackers can use it to trick the original AI into making dangerous mistakes or revealing sensitive information about its internal logic. The paper also suggests ways to protect these AI systems from being copied or manipulated in this manner.

As online news reading has grown, so has the spread of false stories, so these researchers built an automatic system to help identify fake news. Their approach runs articles through three common language tools—a paraphrasing website (Spinbot), a grammar checker (Grammarly), and a technique that translates word meanings into numbers a computer can analyze (GloVe)—and the patterns these tools reveal act as clues about whether a story is genuine. This simple combination performed as well as or better than existing fake-news detectors on standard test datasets, and it held up better when applied to news topics different from those it was originally trained on.

This paper shows that the same kind of “copying” attacks used to steal regular machine learning models can also be used against AI systems that learn through trial and error (deep reinforcement learning). The authors demonstrate that by simply observing and imitating the decisions of these AI agents, an attacker can build a replica of the original policy without needing to see its inner workings. They also provide proof-of-concept examples showing how this copied knowledge can be used to trick or sabotage the original AI, and they discuss possible ways to defend against such attacks.

AI chatbots that answer questions by searching through databases need to translate your everyday language into computer code, but teaching them to do this usually requires massive amounts of training data that is hard and slow to collect. This paper introduces a new, faster method for generating the back-and-forth conversation data needed to train these AI systems. The researchers proved their approach works by successfully using it to train two advanced AI models on different types of databases.

This research introduces a new method to quickly create training data for AI chatbots, solving the common problem of needing massive, hard-to-find datasets to teach computers how to translate human questions into database queries. By automatically generating realistic multi-turn conversations, the system allows developers to train models more efficiently without manually collecting extensive examples. The authors tested this approach on different types of databases and found it successfully improves how well AI assistants can answer user questions using natural language.

This paper addresses the challenge of building AI assistants that can answer questions from databases, which normally requires lots of expensive, hard-to-collect training data. The authors introduce a new method to quickly generate realistic, multi-turn conversational training examples for teaching AI models how to translate everyday language into database queries. They demonstrate that their generated data works well by training two leading models on different database query languages, showing the approach is both effective and flexible.

When patients leave the hospital, staff must manually translate their diagnoses into standardized billing codes (called ICD10 codes), which is slow, tedious work that's hard to automate because medical records are messy and there are thousands of possible codes. The researchers built an AI system that combines multiple machine learning models drawing on different parts of a patient's medical record—not just discharge notes—to predict these codes, and it also indicates how confident it is in each prediction. When tested on real patient data from a hospital in Thailand, the system correctly predicted the main diagnosis about 71% of the time for hospitalized patients and 40% for outpatients, showing real promise while still leaving room for improvement.

This paper introduces a way to hide a secret "signature" inside AI systems that learn by trial and error, much like embedding a hidden watermark in a photograph. The signature is designed to only reveal itself when the AI experiences a specific sequence of events, allowing the original creators to prove ownership if someone steals their work or to safely shut the system down if needed. The researchers tested this idea on a simple AI trained to balance a virtual pole, and it worked without hurting the AI's normal performance.

This paper presents a way to embed a hidden “watermark” into an AI trained to make decisions (a deep reinforcement learning policy), so that the AI will only reveal a special, pre-programmed behavior when it encounters a specific sequence of situations. This watermark has almost no effect on the AI’s normal performance, but it lets owners prove if someone copied their AI or remotely shut it down if needed. The authors tested their method on a simple control task (balancing a virtual pole) and showed it works.

Researchers have developed a method to embed a hidden digital signature into AI decision-making models, allowing owners to prove their work hasn't been stolen or copied. This "watermark" is triggered by specific actions and doesn't significantly reduce the AI's ability to perform its original tasks effectively. It also gives authorized users a way to safely shut down or pause these AI systems if needed.

This paper shows that AI systems that learn skills through trial and error—like those trained to play games or control robots—can be effectively "stolen" by attackers who repeatedly interact with them, observe their behavior, and use those observations to train a copycat AI. The researchers demonstrate that this stolen knowledge can also be weaponized to subtly sabotage the original AI, tricking it into making bad decisions without ever needing access to its internal code. Finally, the authors sketch out possible defenses against these kinds of attacks.

When computers try to figure out "who spoke when" in a recording, they often struggle with moments where two people talk over each other. This research combines two different methods: one that is good at separating many speakers but misses overlaps, and another that handles overlaps well but only works for two voices at a time. By repeatedly using the two-voice method to double-check and fix pairs of speakers identified by the first method, the researchers created a system that performs better than current top tools on several standard audio tests.

Chatbots that answer questions by pulling information from databases need to translate plain English questions into database query languages, but teaching AI systems to do this normally requires huge amounts of example data that is slow and expensive to create. The researchers built a tool that quickly generates realistic, multi-turn conversations (like a back-and-forth dialogue with an assistant) to build these training datasets much faster. To prove their generated data works, they used it to train two leading AI models on two different types of database query languages, showing the approach is both effective and adaptable.

This research combines two different methods for identifying who is speaking in a recording to better handle situations where people talk over each other. By using a specialized tool to refine the results of a standard clustering method, the new approach fixes errors that occur when multiple speakers overlap or when there are many participants. Tests on various audio datasets show that this hybrid technique consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems.

This paper is about improving technology that identifies who is speaking when in an audio recording with multiple people. Traditional methods work by grouping parts of the audio into separate speakers, but they struggle when two people talk at the same time. The researchers propose a fix: after the traditional method finishes, they use a second, more specialized tool that focuses on pairs of speakers to clean up and correct overlapping speech. Their experiments show this two-step approach consistently makes the overall results more accurate across several standard test datasets.

This research introduces a free, virtual reality driving simulator that allows scientists to study how distracted drivers react when they need to suddenly take control of an automated vehicle. By providing a realistic 25-square-kilometer environment with traffic and pedestrians, the toolkit lets researchers test different warning systems without needing expensive, bulky physical simulators. Essentially, it offers an affordable and flexible way for anyone to investigate safer ways for humans and self-driving cars to interact.

As self-driving cars become more common, passengers will likely do other things while riding but still need to quickly take the wheel when the car asks them to. To study how people safely handle this transition, researchers built a free, highly realistic virtual reality driving world—complete with traffic, pedestrians, and steering wheels that vibrate to mimic real driving. This open toolkit lets scientists run these experiments easily and affordably without needing expensive, bulky driving simulators.

This paper introduces a free virtual reality tool that lets researchers study how drivers react when a self-driving car suddenly asks them to take back control. Built using the Unity game engine, the toolkit includes a large, realistic virtual city with cars, pedestrians, and nature, along with support for steering wheels with force feedback and eye-tracking devices. Its goal is to provide a low-cost, flexible alternative to expensive driving simulators, making it easier for scientists to run experiments on driver attention and takeover situations.

The researchers developed a way to embed a hidden signature into AI systems that learn skills through trial and error, so that the AI gives a special, prearranged response when it encounters a specific sequence of situations—without hurting how well it performs its normal job. This hidden signature works like a watermark on a photo: it lets the original creator prove ownership if someone steals or copies their AI, and it can also act as a built-in "off switch" that allows authorized people to interrupt or stop the AI's behavior. The team demonstrated that this works by testing it on a classic benchmark task where an AI learns to keep a pole balanced on a moving cart.

Researchers compared three modern artificial intelligence methods for turning speech into text to see which works best when using large amounts of data. They found that while one method is superior for processing complete audio files, another performs well for real-time conversations if set up correctly, and a third "Transformer" model achieved the highest accuracy in both scenarios. Ultimately, these new end-to-end models outperformed older, highly optimized hybrid systems, suggesting they are more effective for future voice recognition technology.

Researchers tested three modern AI methods that convert spoken words directly into text, training them on a massive 65,000 hours of audio to see which performs best. They found that while one method (Transformer-AED) was the most accurate overall, another method (RNN-T) works really well for real-time tasks like live captioning if set up correctly. Ultimately, both of these newer approaches outperformed the older, traditional technology used for speech recognition.

This paper compares three modern AI methods for turning speech into text, using a huge amount of Microsoft voice data to test them fairly. The researchers found that one method (Transformer-AED) was the most accurate overall, while another (RNN-T) performed almost as well when processing speech in real time. Importantly, these newer “end-to-end” approaches can outperform the older, carefully tuned hybrid systems, especially with large datasets.

Researchers wanted to see if AI could better figure out people's positions on controversial topics by teaching it to recognize the emotions and feelings behind their words. To do this, they built a new collection of arguments for and against 419 different issues, like those you might see on a debate website. They discovered that a surprisingly simple AI tool could perform just as well as much larger, more complex models while using far less computing power, and it can even highlight exactly which phrases helped it understand someone's stance.

As self-driving cars become more advanced, people will spend time on other activities while being driven, so researchers want to know how a distracted person can safely take back control when the car asks them to. To study this, the researchers created a free, open-source virtual reality driving simulation—built with video game technology—that includes realistic traffic, pedestrians, and a large city environment, and even works with force-feedback steering wheels and eye-tracking. Because it runs on affordable VR equipment instead of bulky, expensive driving simulators, it gives researchers around the world a cheap and flexible way to test how humans respond when an automated car hands control back to them.

**What the paper is about, in plain language:**

The paper tackles the problem of figuring out *who is speaking when* in an audio recording, which is especially hard when people talk over each other—traditional methods can only assign each moment to a single speaker, so overlapping speech gets mislabeled. The researchers combine two existing techniques: they first use the traditional approach to get a rough map of all the speakers, then apply a neural network trained to separate just two voices at a time, repeatedly picking pairs of speakers and cleaning up the moments where those two overlap. When tested on three standard collections of real recorded conversations, this hybrid method consistently outperformed the best existing approaches, showing that each technique can cover for the other's weaknesses.

Researchers built a new dataset of 419 controversial topics to test how well AI can determine if someone supports or opposes an issue. They found that a simpler, less complex model using emotion data performed nearly as well as much larger, advanced models while being far more efficient. Additionally, they developed a method to clearly show which specific words in a text help the AI make its decision.

This paper tests whether AI language models can better identify people’s positions (for or against) on hot-button topics when the models also consider the emotions or opinions expressed in the text. The researchers built a new dataset of arguments on 419 controversial issues, and they found that a much smaller, simpler model using sentiment or emotion cues can perform nearly as well as a large, complex model like BERT. They also created a method to show which specific phrases in a text most influenced the model’s stance prediction.

This study compares three modern "all-in-one" neural network approaches for turning spoken words into written text, training them on a massive dataset of 65,000 hours of speech. The researchers found that a Transformer-based approach achieved the best accuracy overall, whether transcribing complete recordings or live speech as it happens. Importantly, even in real-time streaming mode, two of these new approaches beat a highly-optimized traditional speech recognition system, suggesting the newer technology is ready to replace older methods.

This research looks at how to keep wireless communication strong and reliable between humans and robots working together in automated warehouses, which is essential for preventing accidents. The researchers used computer simulations of a warehouse filled with metal shelving to test how well a specific type of radio signal travels around obstacles. Based on those tests, they created practical guidelines for where to place antennas on both people and robots so their safety signals don’t get blocked or weakened.

This study uses computer simulations to test how well wireless signals travel between humans and robots in a warehouse filled with metal shelves. The researchers analyzed signal strength under various conditions to understand how the environment affects communication reliability. Based on these findings, they provide recommendations for placing antennas on workers and robots to ensure clear signals that help prevent collisions.

This paper studies how wireless signals travel through a busy warehouse where people and robots work together, to make sure they can always communicate and avoid crashing into each other. The researchers used computer simulations to model the warehouse shelves as metal blocks and tested how the signal strength changes in different situations. Based on these results, they recommend the best places to put antennas on both people and robots to keep their communication reliable and safe.

This study tackles the problem of teaching computers to automatically figure out whether a piece of text is for or against a controversial topic, using a new dataset the authors built from procon.org containing arguments on both sides of 419 hot-button issues. Surprisingly, they found that a fairly small and simple AI model—especially one given clues about the sentiment and emotion in the text—could perform about as well as a much larger, cutting-edge language model (BERT) while using 20 times fewer internal parameters. The researchers also developed a straightforward way to show which specific words or phrases drove the model's judgment, making its decisions easier for people to understand.

Robots struggle to move fast because their sensors can only see a short distance ahead, and processing that information takes too much computing power. To solve this, researchers taught a robot to use artificial intelligence to predict what the area beyond its "vision" looks like, allowing it to plan its path more effectively without needing humans to manually label training data. When tested on a physical race-car-style robot, this prediction method helped it navigate safely at higher speeds than standard approaches.

Researchers developed an AI system that allows robots to "imagine" obstacles and open spaces beyond what their cameras can currently see, helping them navigate safely at high speeds. This method uses a neural network trained on real-world data to predict the layout of areas outside the robot's direct line of sight, overcoming the limitations of standard sensors. Tests with a physical racing car showed that this predictive approach significantly improved navigation performance compared to systems that rely only on visible data.

This paper addresses the challenge of helping robots move quickly and safely by overcoming two problems: the slow process of building maps and the limited range of their sensors. The researchers trained an artificial intelligence system to predict what lies beyond the robot’s immediate sensor range, using real-world data without needing humans to label it. They then updated the robot’s control software to use these predictions, and in tests with a physical robot car moving at 4 meters per second, their approach performed better than one relying only on direct sensor readings.

This study uses computer simulations to examine how a special type of wireless signal (ultrawideband) travels through a warehouse where humans and robots work side by side, so they can constantly track each other's locations and avoid dangerous collisions. The researchers modeled the warehouse's metal shelving as clusters of metal boxes and calculated how the signals bounce off surfaces and weaken as they travel, including how the roughness of the racks affects reception. Based on these results, they recommend the best spots to attach the wireless devices on workers' bodies and on robots to keep the communication link strong and the workplace safe.

This research tested different computer programs that mimic evolution to solve problems, specifically looking at how they automatically adjust their "mutation rate"—the amount of random change introduced to find better solutions. The researchers discovered that which program works best depends heavily on how many new variations it generates at each step: one method wins when generating only a few variations, while a different method takes the lead when generating many. They also found that setting a minimum limit on how much random change is allowed affects performance, and the ideal limit flips depending on whether the program is making a small or large number of variations.

This study finds that the best method for tuning an evolutionary algorithm's "mutation rate" depends heavily on how many new solutions are generated in each step. While simple static settings work well for small groups, more complex self-adjusting methods become superior as the group size increases. Therefore, choosing the right algorithm requires matching its complexity to the specific population size being used.

This paper compares different versions of evolutionary algorithms—computer programs that improve solutions over time, inspired by natural selection—to see which one solves a simple optimization problem fastest. The researchers found that the best algorithm depends heavily on how many “offspring” (candidate solutions) are generated each round: with small groups, one method wins, but with larger groups, another method takes over, and there’s even a middle ground where a simpler, non-adjusting method ties with the best. They also discovered that the minimum allowed mutation rate (how often small random changes occur) matters differently depending on the group size, with a more permissive lower limit helping for small groups but hurting for large ones.

Researchers developed a new AI model that automatically assigns standard medical diagnostic codes to patients by analyzing only their prescribed medications, simplifying the typically complex and data-heavy coding process. Tested on real hospital records, this approach successfully predicted diagnoses for both inpatient and outpatient cases, offering a more efficient solution than previous methods that required extensive data sources. This innovation could help hospitals streamline administrative tasks like billing and research while overcoming challenges related to limited or inconsistent digital health data.

Hospitals use a standard set of codes to officially record patient diagnoses for tasks like billing and medical research, but doing this manually is slow and difficult. The researchers built an artificial intelligence tool that can automatically predict these diagnosis codes just by looking at the medications a doctor prescribed. They tested it on real hospital records and found it was reasonably accurate, especially for patients who were admitted to the hospital rather than just visiting a clinic.

Fast-moving robots are held back by their sensors, which can only see a limited area around them—too little information to plan safely at high speeds. The researchers solved this by training a computer model to predict what the terrain ahead looks like beyond the robot's camera range, learning this skill automatically from real-world data without any human labeling. When tested on a physical robot race car, this predictive approach allowed it to navigate collision-free at 4 meters per second (about 9 mph) noticeably better than a robot relying only on what it could directly see.

This paper describes a computer system that automatically assigns medical billing codes (ICD10) to patient records using only their prescription information, rather than requiring full medical charts. The researchers developed a new machine learning method called "collaborative residual learning" and tested it on real hospital data from Thailand, covering both hospitalized patients and clinic visitors. Their system was able to predict the main diagnosis with moderate success—performing better for inpatients than outpatients—which is notable because it works with just medication data, making it more practical across different healthcare settings.

This paper introduces MobileNetV3, a new version of artificial intelligence software designed to run fast and efficiently on mobile phones. The researchers used automated search tools combined with clever design tweaks to build two models—one for powerful phones and one for basic devices—that can quickly recognize objects and understand what’s happening in photos. These new models are both faster and more accurate than the previous version, setting a new performance record for AI tasks like image recognition, object detection, and scene analysis on mobile devices.

Researchers have developed new, efficient artificial intelligence models called MobileNetV3 that are specifically optimized to run quickly on mobile phone processors. By combining automated search algorithms with innovative design techniques, these models achieve higher accuracy while using less battery power and running faster than their predecessors. This advancement allows for better performance in common smartphone tasks like recognizing objects in photos and analyzing scenes, setting a new standard for mobile AI efficiency.

This paper introduces a new version of MobileNet, a type of efficient AI model designed to run quickly on smartphones and other devices with limited computing power. The researchers used automated search methods combined with manual design improvements to create two models: one for powerful phones and one for budget devices. The new models are faster and more accurate than the previous version across several tasks, including recognizing objects in photos and identifying every pixel in an image.

Researchers created a new method that uses artificial intelligence to quickly and accurately predict indoor air quality by combining computer simulations with real-time data from sensors. They tested this approach by tracking carbon dioxide (CO2) levels in an enclosed space. Ultimately, this technology could be used to monitor airborne viruses like the one that causes COVID-19 in real time, since virus levels in the air are closely linked to CO2 concentrations.

Researchers have developed a new AI method to accurately and quickly monitor indoor air quality, such as CO2 levels, by combining machine learning with real-time sensor data. This approach simplifies complex environmental models using neural networks, allowing for faster predictions that can help estimate the risk of airborne viruses like SARS-CoV-2 in enclosed spaces.

This paper introduces a new method that combines machine learning with real sensor data to better predict indoor air quality, which is important for health. The approach uses a type of artificial intelligence to simplify the problem and create a fast, approximate model of how air pollutants like CO2 change over time, then updates this model with actual measurements to keep it accurate. The technique was tested on CO2 levels indoors and could potentially be used to estimate the amount of viruses in the air, such as the one causing COVID-19, based on CO2 readings.

The researchers created a new AI model called MobileNetV3 that runs efficiently on smartphone processors, and rather than designing it entirely by hand, they used automated search algorithms—essentially letting computers help design the AI architecture—to find the best design. They released two versions: a "Large" model for more powerful devices and a "Small" one for simpler devices, both of which are more accurate and faster than the previous version. The models were also adapted for other visual tasks, like spotting objects in photos and labeling what every part of an image is, achieving top performance among mobile AI systems.

When patients are diagnosed, hospitals must translate each diagnosis into standardized codes (called ICD10) for billing and medical research—a task traditionally done manually. This study developed a machine-learning system that predicts these codes automatically using only the medications a doctor prescribed, based on the idea that the drugs someone receives are strong clues to their underlying illness. Tested on real patient data from a Thai hospital, the system correctly identified the primary diagnosis about 73% of the time for admitted patients and 44% for outpatient visits, suggesting prescriptions alone can be a useful shortcut for automating this administrative work.

Researchers have created a new interactive app that helps both deaf and hearing people learn Greek Sign Language, English Sign Language, and how to translate between the two. The app acts like a dictionary where users can look up signs alphabetically, see their meanings, read the written words, and even hear the pronunciation if they have some hearing left. Rather than just being a simple reference tool, it actively helps users practice and remember what they’ve learned through fun quizzes that use text and videos.

This paper describes a new app designed to help both deaf and hearing people learn Greek Sign Language and English Sign Language. The app shows signs in alphabetical order, displays their written words and meanings, plays audio for users with partial hearing, and includes quizzes to test what users have learned. Unlike a simple dictionary, the platform is interactive, allowing users to actively practice and reinforce their sign language skills.

Researchers have developed an interactive app that helps people learn and translate between Greek and English Sign Languages, going beyond a simple dictionary by including practice exercises. The platform uses videos, audio cues for those with partial hearing loss, and multiple-choice quizzes to actively teach users how signs work. This tool aims to improve communication skills for both deaf and hearing individuals through engaging, hands-on learning experiences.

Evolutionary algorithms are problem-solving techniques inspired by biological evolution: they randomly "mutate" candidate solutions, keep the best ones, and this study compares several strategies for automatically adjusting how aggressively those mutations occur. The main finding is that the best strategy depends on how many mutated offspring the algorithm produces each round—with small batches, one method (the "2-rate" rule) is most efficient, but once batches exceed roughly 50–100 offspring, a different method (multiplicative updates, which scale the rate up or down by fixed factors) wins, and around 50 offspring even a plain fixed mutation rate performs just as well as the smarter self-adjusting approaches. The researchers also show that the minimum allowed mutation rate matters: allowing a very small minimum works better when batches are small, while enforcing a stricter minimum is better for large batches.

The researchers developed a fast AI-based computer model that predicts how air quality—specifically CO2 levels—changes inside a room over time, using machine learning to keep the calculations simple enough to run in real time. To make its predictions more accurate, the model is continuously corrected using live measurements from real sensors in the space, rather than relying on simulations alone. Because CO2 levels can act as a proxy for how much exhaled air (and potentially viruses like the one that causes COVID-19) is lingering in a room, this tool could one day give people real-time warnings when indoor air becomes risky to breathe.

Researchers developed a system that helps robots learn inspection tasks from human demonstrations by creating clear, computer-generated instructions that explain the robot’s decisions. This approach allows the robot to not only perform tasks in new environments but also provide understandable reasons for its actions and identify why it might fail. By combining machine learning with program synthesis, the method makes autonomous systems more transparent and easier to verify than traditional "black box" AI models.

Researchers developed a system that teaches a robot how to do inspection tasks by watching a human perform them, combining that demonstration with smart pattern recognition so the robot needs less hands-on training. Unlike many AI systems that act like mysterious "black boxes," this approach translates what the robot learns into clear, readable instructions and allows it to explain its own decisions or why it made a mistake. The team successfully tested this on a wheeled robot, proving it could not only learn from a demonstration but also write its own new plans to navigate and inspect areas in environments it had never seen before.

This paper describes an app that teaches both Greek and English Sign Language to people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or fully hearing. Users can look up signs organized alphabetically, see the written word and its meaning, hear how the word sounds (helpful for those with partial hearing), and translate between the two sign languages. Unlike a simple dictionary, the app also includes interactive quizzes with text and video, so learners can actively practice and test what they've learned.

This paper describes a system that lets a robot learn inspection tasks by watching a human demonstrate them, then figuring out the important goals and steps on its own. The robot creates a simple, readable program from these demonstrations, which it can then use to perform inspections in new environments it hasn't seen before. The system can also explain its decisions and identify what went wrong if something fails, making the robot's behavior easier for people to understand and trust.

This research explores how to better predict when and how much individual users will use their cell phones, which helps mobile networks manage their resources more efficiently. The researchers tested different prediction methods—from basic math formulas to advanced artificial intelligence—on real data and found that AI works best when there is plenty of past usage history, while simpler methods are actually better when only a little history is available. Ultimately, they showed that accurately predicting user activity allows the network to prepare in advance, significantly reducing lag and delays for the user.

Researchers are developing smarter ways to predict how much data users will send and receive over cellular networks, helping providers manage resources more efficiently. They found that simple statistical methods work best for short-term predictions, while complex machine learning becomes superior once enough past data is available. By accurately forecasting this traffic, network operators can proactively adjust their systems to reduce delays and improve user experience.

This paper looks at ways to predict how much data a cellphone user will need, which helps networks manage their resources more efficiently. The researchers tested different prediction methods—ranging from simple statistical rules to advanced deep learning—and found that the best choice depends on how far ahead you want to predict and what information you use. They also showed that predicting data usage can help reduce delays, and they explored identifying which apps are being used just from traffic patterns.

Researchers have proven that two popular algorithms for solving complex optimization problems converge to a solution at a predictable, efficient rate. By showing these methods act like simplified versions of a standard mathematical technique, the study provides the first clear proof of how fast one specific algorithm works in broad scenarios. This finding helps computer scientists and mathematicians better understand and apply these tools for tasks like training AI models or balancing competing objectives.

This paper studies two popular mathematical algorithms used to find the optimal balance point in problems where one side is trying to minimize a value while the other is trying to maximize it. The researchers discovered that both methods are essentially clever shortcuts for simulating a slower, more idealized approach, which guarantees that their calculations stay stable and don't spiral out of control. As a result, they proved mathematically that these algorithms reliably zero in on the correct answer at a predictable speed—specifically, the error shrinks proportionally as you divide one by the number of steps taken—which provides the first formal guarantee of this kind for one of the methods.

This paper looks at two popular algorithms used to find the best solution in competitive optimization problems, where one side tries to maximize a score while the other tries to minimize it. The authors show that both methods can be understood as simplified versions of a more fundamental, but computationally expensive, “ideal” algorithm. Using this new perspective, they prove that the average of the solutions found by these algorithms gets closer to the true optimal balance point at a predictable and steady rate, even for a broad class of problems that were previously difficult to analyze.

This study develops tools to predict how much data individual mobile phone users will send and receive, comparing simple statistical methods against advanced AI (deep learning) approaches. A key finding is a practical trade-off: deep learning becomes more accurate when there's plenty of past data to learn from, while simpler statistical methods actually work better when only a short history is available. The researchers also showed that traffic patterns alone can reveal which app is generating the data (without inspecting the content itself), and that predicting when traffic will arrive lets the network prepare resources in advance, reducing delays for users.

The researchers developed a system that lets a robot learn how to inspect an environment by watching a human operator demonstrate the task, rather than being programmed step-by-step. Unlike most AI systems that learn in ways humans can't easily understand, this one produces a readable computer program that can be checked and verified, and it can explain its decisions—including pinpointing what caused a failure after the fact. When tested on a ground vehicle that had to inspect different areas in a specific order, the robot successfully performed the task in a new environment it had never seen before, while explaining its choices along the way.

Online stores often struggle to keep inappropriate images—like those containing violence, offensive logos, or explicit content—from appearing in their product listings, especially when outside sellers are uploading them. To solve this, the researchers built a smart computer system that can automatically scan and flag bad images across massive online catalogs. They combined advanced image-recognition technology with human reviewers to overcome common challenges, like not having enough examples of bad images to teach the software effectively.

This paper describes a computer system that automatically scans product photos on shopping websites to flag ones that contain inappropriate or rule-breaking content, like violent imagery, offensive symbols, or unauthorized promotional logos. The authors explain the technical difficulties of building such a system, including having very few examples of bad images to learn from and dealing with an enormous, constantly changing catalog of products. Their solution combines advanced image recognition technology with targeted human review to keep online marketplaces safe and trustworthy for shoppers.

Researchers want to make AI language tools more trustworthy by understanding *why* they make certain predictions, but current ways of testing this understanding often rely on subjective human opinions. To fix this, the authors created a new testing task where the "correct" explanation for an AI's decision is built directly into the rules of the problem itself, removing human bias. They are releasing this unbiased test as a standard benchmark so other researchers can fairly measure how well different methods explain AI decisions.

Researchers created a new test called QUACKIE to evaluate how well artificial intelligence can explain its own decisions in language tasks. Unlike previous methods that rely on human opinions, this benchmark uses questions with objectively correct answers to provide clear, unbiased proof of whether an AI's explanation is accurate. This approach helps scientists better measure and improve the trustworthiness of AI models by giving them a reliable standard for testing interpretability.

This paper examines two popular step-by-step algorithms for solving "min-max" problems—situations where two parties have opposing goals, one trying to minimize an outcome and the other trying to maximize it, as arises in games, economics, and adversarial machine learning. The authors' key insight is that both algorithms can be viewed as practical approximations of an idealized but computationally impractical method (the "proximal point method"), and this perspective lets them prove the algorithms stay on track and reliably approach a solution. As a result, they show that the error shrinks in proportion to 1 divided by the number of steps taken—so doubling the effort roughly halves the error—and notably, this is the first time such a speed guarantee has been proven for the OGDA algorithm in this general setting.

This paper introduces a new way to test how well we can understand and trust AI language models. Instead of relying on people to manually label what the “right” explanation should be, the researchers created a special task where the correct explanation is automatically known from how the task itself is designed. They then use this setup as a benchmark to compare how well different existing methods for explaining AI decisions actually perform.

Online marketplaces host millions of product photos from many different sellers, and some of these images contain offensive or rule-breaking content—such as violent, sexual, racist, or unauthorized promotional material—that can harm shoppers' experience and create legal problems for the company. The researchers built an AI system that automatically scans enormous collections of product images to flag this problematic content, something human reviewers couldn't keep up with at that scale. To make the system work despite challenges like having very few examples of the offending images to learn from, they combined modern image-recognition technology with feedback from crowdsourced human reviewers.

Whole-body MRI scans are crucial for detecting cancer in children, but standard AI tools fail because they cannot handle the unique challenges of pediatric imaging, such as growing bones and movement during scans. Researchers tested new AI techniques called generative models to create high-quality synthetic images that mimic real pediatric scans, overcoming these data limitations. They found that a specific model, StyleGAN2, produced the most realistic and useful images when evaluated by both computer metrics and human experts.

Catching cancer early is especially important for children, but getting clear full-body MRI scans from young kids is difficult because they move around and their bodies are constantly growing. To help solve this problem, researchers used a type of artificial intelligence to create realistic, computer-generated practice images based on real scans from a children's hospital. They found that one specific AI tool was excellent at producing these fake medical images, which could eventually help doctors build better technology to detect childhood cancers without needing as many hard-to-get real scans.

This paper looks at using artificial intelligence to create realistic whole-body MRI scans for children, which could help improve early cancer detection. The researchers faced challenges because children's bones change as they grow, it's hard to get young kids to stay still during scans, and there aren't many examples of scans showing cancer in children. They tested different AI models and found that one called StyleGAN2 produced the most realistic-looking images, which they confirmed through both computer measurements and review by a radiology expert.

When AI language models make predictions, researchers want tools that can explain *why* the model gave a particular answer—but it's hard to judge how good these explanation tools are, because existing test datasets rely on human-written "correct" explanations that may be biased. The authors solved this by building a special classification task out of question-answering data, where the right explanation is baked into the definition of the task itself, so no subjective human judgment is needed. Using this setup, they tested how well many of today's leading explanation methods actually perform, creating a reliable yardstick for future research.

Researchers have developed a privacy-friendly system using low-cost infrared sensors to automatically monitor people in public spaces for both physical distancing and elevated body temperatures. This technology works passively without requiring individuals to carry devices or cooperate, making it suitable for crowded areas like hospitals, offices, and homes. By combining movement tracking with health screening, the system helps ensure safety and supports early detection of potential disease outbreaks while protecting user privacy.

This research describes a system that uses inexpensive heat-sensing cameras to monitor crowded spaces, checking whether people are keeping a safe distance from one another and if anyone has an unusually high body temperature. Unlike smartphone tracking apps, these sensors work completely passively by just detecting the natural heat bodies give off, so they don’t require people to do anything or sacrifice their privacy. The researchers developed software to connect these sensors together, allowing them to automatically track where people are moving and spot potential signs of illness in places like workplaces, hospitals, or public buildings.

Online stores use artificial intelligence to automatically scan millions of product images for offensive or rule-breaking content, such as violent or sexually explicit material. Because these harmful images can damage a brand’s reputation and lead to legal problems, the system employs specialized techniques to identify them accurately despite having limited examples to learn from. This scalable solution helps retailers maintain a safe shopping experience by catching inappropriate listings before customers ever see them.

This paper presents a system that uses low-cost thermal sensors to automatically monitor people in public spaces for two purposes: tracking how far apart they are and checking whether anyone has a fever. The sensors work passively, meaning they don’t require people to carry phones or give consent, and they don’t capture identifying images, so privacy is preserved. The authors describe how to process the heat signals to locate people, measure distances between them, and flag abnormal body temperatures, testing the approach in real-world settings like offices or shared living areas.

Humans can usually figure out what a new word means just by looking at the words around it, even if they've only seen it once, but teaching computers to learn this way is still very difficult. In this study, researchers tested different mathematical methods for helping an AI guess missing words after seeing only one, two, or three examples. They discovered that no single method works best every time—the right approach actually changes depending on how many examples the computer gets—and they created a standard test using public data so future researchers can easily compare their own AI tools.

Researchers developed a new method that allows computers to learn the meaning of a word from just one or two examples, mimicking how humans understand new vocabulary through context. They discovered that there is no single best mathematical formula for measuring similarity between words; instead, the most effective approach changes depending on how many examples are available during training. This work also provides a standardized public dataset and benchmark so other scientists can easily test and compare their own language-learning models in the future.

Children at risk of cancer often need frequent whole-body MRI scans, but building AI tools to help analyze these scans is difficult because kids' bodies change as they grow, young children struggle to stay still during imaging, and examples of actual cancer in these scans are rare. The researchers tested whether AI image-generation technology (known as generative adversarial networks) could create realistic synthetic whole-body MRI scans of children, which could help fill the gap where real data is scarce. Using both automated quality measures and a review by a radiologist, they found that one particular model, StyleGAN2, produced the most realistic-looking scans.

This paper looks at how computers can learn the meaning of a new word from just one or a few examples, similar to how people do when they encounter unfamiliar words in context. The researchers tested different mathematical ways of measuring similarity between words to see which works best when learning from only one, two, or three examples. Their main findings are that no single measurement method is always the best—it depends on how many examples are used—and they provide a standard test setup so other researchers can compare future results on this task.

This paper presents a system of low-cost infrared (heat-detecting) sensors, mounted on walls or ceilings, that can monitor people in crowded public spaces to check whether they're keeping a safe distance from one another and whether anyone has an unusually high body temperature. Unlike contact-tracing apps or regular cameras, these sensors are completely passive—people don't need to carry a phone or be identified in any way—so the system can help catch potential illness outbreaks without raising privacy concerns. The authors developed the mathematical and signal-processing methods needed to combine distance tracking and fever screening, and they tested the approach with real-world measurements in different setups, from factories to homes and shared spaces.

This study explores what makes people trust self-driving cars, using survey answers from over a thousand participants about their knowledge, feelings, and views on risks and benefits. The researchers used a machine learning model to predict trust based on these answers, and then applied a special tool to explain why the model made its predictions. Their approach proved better than older methods at both accurately predicting trust and clearly explaining the reasons behind it.

Researchers surveyed over 1,100 people to understand what drives trust in self-driving cars, analyzing factors like personal knowledge, risk perception, and past experiences.
