Researchers built a new test to see if AI language models actually understand why they make certain decisions. Instead of asking people to judge the AI's explanations—which can be biased—they used the clear rules of a question-answering task to automatically verify whether the AI was thinking correctly. This creates a fairer, more objective way to measure how trustworthy AI systems really are.

E-commerce companies struggle to automatically catch offensive or non-compliant images in product listings, since these can include anything from violent imagery to unauthorized logos across millions of products. The researchers built an AI system that uses advanced computer vision techniques to detect problematic images at scale. Their approach combines state-of-the-art machine learning with crowdsourced human review to handle the challenges of limited training data and the constantly changing nature of online product catalogs.

This research is about using AI to create realistic whole-body MRI scans for children. The researchers used a special type of AI (called StyleGAN2) that generates images, and found it could create convincing children's MRI scans based on real data from a Toronto children's hospital. This could help doctors detect cancer earlier in children by improving the quality of MRI scans, which is especially challenging for kids who have trouble staying still during scans.

The paper presents a low-cost system that uses passive infrared thermal-sensor arrays to monitor people in public spaces without needing their cooperation or risking their privacy. It combines motion tracking to measure social-distancing behaviors with automated body-temperature screening to spot potential signs of illness. Designed for flexible deployment in both public and private settings, the approach offers a scalable, non-invasive tool for improving safety and enabling early outbreak response.

This paper tries to teach AI language models to learn new words from just a few examples, much like humans can guess a word's meaning from context even on first encounter. The researchers tested different mathematical methods for comparing words to see which worked best when the AI had only one, two, or three chances to learn, discovering that no single method works best for every situation. They also created a public benchmark using Wikipedia text so other researchers can measure and compare progress on this challenging few-shot learning problem.

This paper is about a better way for banks to divide their customers into meaningful groups. The researchers created a system called Customer2Vec that turns customer information into a special code, which helps a computer understand what makes customers similar or different. This allows banks to more accurately group customers, making it easier to offer them the right products and services.

The researchers surveyed over a thousand people about their attitudes and experiences with self-driving cars, then used a sophisticated computer algorithm to predict how much those individuals would trust the vehicles. Their model was designed to be highly accurate while also being transparent enough to show exactly which factors—like safety fears or technical knowledge—drove each prediction. This demonstrates that artificial intelligence can help us understand and forecast public trust in automated cars without sacrificing clear explanations.

This paper looks at a way to automatically assign standard medical diagnosis codes (ICD-10) using only the list of medications a patient was prescribed. The researchers created a new machine learning model that helps improve predictions by learning from shared patterns in the data. Their tests on real hospital records show the method works reasonably well, suggesting prescriptions alone can help automate an important but difficult hospital task.

This paper reviews how a powerful statistical tool called Gaussian Processes (GPs) is used to analyze Earth observation data, like satellite measurements of the environment. GPs help scientists estimate things like vegetation, soil, or climate variables while also measuring how uncertain those estimates are. The authors highlight new methods that make these models more accurate, identify the most important data features, and allow predictions to be reliably applied across different places and times.

This paper is about teaching computers to quickly spot and analyze clothing in images—like identifying a shirt and locating its collar or sleeves. The researchers built a system called DeepMark++ that's much faster and lighter than previous tools, fast enough to run in real time on a smartphone. It performs nearly as well as the best existing systems and even won second place in a major fashion AI competition.

Researchers wanted to help detect chronic kidney disease early in a Nigerian community where it has become common, so they trained an artificial intelligence system to recognize the illness using medical records from 400 patients. The AI learned to predict whether a patient has kidney disease with 98% accuracy by analyzing 10 different health measurements from blood tests and exams. Most importantly, the study revealed that two specific substances in the blood—creatinine and bicarbonate—are the strongest warning signs, which could help doctors identify at-risk patients sooner.

This paper shows that a popular security tool called "fuzzy commitments" fails to protect the digital face scans used by modern facial recognition systems. Because these systems create face data that is too predictable, the researchers successfully reverse-engineered the protected codes to reconstruct the original faces. These reconstructions were so accurate that they could bypass security locks up to 78% of the time, even when used on different systems than the one that created them.

Cyber attacks on computers and smart devices are growing every year, so researchers built a tool that helps pick the best algorithm to detect these attacks on a network. Instead of relying on slow trial-and-error, their system uses data characteristics and user input to recommend the most suitable detection method. Testing showed that their approaches work well, consistently suggesting strong algorithms even if not always the single best one.

Data scientists must pick many options—like how to clean data and which algorithm to use—when building a machine learning model, and the number of combinations grows huge fast. This paper presents an AutoML system that automatically finds a good pipeline using math tools (matrix and tensor factorization) as simplified stand-ins for all those choices. It then uses smart strategies to test options efficiently, and tests show it works well on many real datasets.

Imagine several robots, like drones, each trying to finish its own job—such as visiting certain places within specific time windows—while sharing the same space. The researchers developed a method where each robot plans its path on the fly, coordinating with others in a decentralized way to avoid crashes. Their approach guarantees that as long as the environment is sufficiently connected, every robot will safely complete its task without getting stuck, possibly with a slight delay.

Researchers built an AI chatbot that can hold longer conversations while staying in character by remembering details like who is speaking, where they are, and what specific topic they're discussing. They upgraded an existing advanced dialogue system (hredGAN) to track these extra identity and context clues, creating a new model called phredGAN. When tested on TV show scripts and customer service chats, this improved version produced more consistent, on-character responses than previous systems.

Researchers are exploring how people can train AI models more efficiently by letting the AI explain its own predictions while learning. However, they found that when the AI picks which examples to study, it may unintentionally choose ones that make itself look more accurate than it really is—creating a misleading impression of its abilities. Their solution flips the roles: the human picks the training examples, while the AI provides global insights to help the person select the most challenging and informative ones.

Researchers are studying how to best set up algorithms so they work well on new, unseen problems, by using a "portfolio" of different settings and picking the best one for each situation. This paper mathematically proves that if you include too many different settings in your portfolio, the system will "overfit"—meaning it becomes too tailored to the practice problems and fails to perform well on future, real-world challenges. Therefore, there is a tricky trade-off: while having more options increases the chance of finding a perfect setting, it also makes it harder to guarantee the algorithm will remain reliable in the long run.

Imagine you have several different decision-making strategies for choosing which option will give the best reward, but you don't know which strategy will work best in advance. This paper describes a smart method that treats each strategy like a slot machine arm, using a simple trial-and-error approach to figure out which one to trust more over time. The result is a combined strategy that performs nearly as well as the best individual strategy would have if you had known which one to pick from the start, without needing the strict conditions that previous methods required.

This paper introduces a new way to read tourist reviews and automatically find specific details about who can or cannot visit a place, such as whether it is wheelchair accessible, has gluten-free options, or is suitable for babies. The researchers built a computer system that scans thousands of reviews to identify these "inclusion" and "exclusion" phrases, successfully spotting them with about 80% accuracy and correctly categorizing them into 11 different visitor needs roughly 97–98% of the time. By pulling these hidden details from reviews, the system could help travel-planning apps automatically warn users if a specific attraction might not work for their particular situation.
